title: Make It Memorable
author: Molly Graham
summary: This article by former Facebook operations leader Molly Graham argues that a goal or value only matters to organizational behavior if someone can remember it in the moment they need to use it — and that most organizations fail this test by setting too many goals and too many values, making all of them forgettable. The core principle is that memorability equals usability: if people can't hold something in their heads, they fall back on their own instincts, their manager's preferences, or whatever feels urgent in the moment. Graham draws on her Facebook experience to illustrate what works: three top-line goals (Growth, Engagement, Revenue) that every person in the company could state and explain. The article makes the case for ruthless simplicity in both goal-setting and values articulation — not because three is a magic number but because the human cognitive limit for reliably carrying a set of things is approximately three. Values that nobody can remember are decorative; goals that require reading a document are not actually guiding decisions.
points: A goal only matters to organizational behavior if someone can remember it at the moment of decision — if your goals require consulting a document, they are not actually guiding how people prioritize their time.

Most organizations fail the memorability test by setting too many goals and too many values: if you have fourteen company values, people will remember three, and they won't all remember the same three.

Three is not a magic number, but it is approximately the cognitive limit for a set of things a person can reliably hold in their head and use in real time — Facebook's three top-line goals (Growth, Engagement, Revenue) worked precisely because everyone could state them without looking anything up.

Values are only working if they help people make decisions when no senior leader is in the room — a value that cannot break a tie between two engineering approaches is decorative, not cultural infrastructure.

Goals are a communication tool, not a planning document: their purpose is to help people decide what to work on, prioritize their time, and know what winning looks like — if they can't do that, they are wasting everyone's time.
quotes: If people can't remember something, they can't use it. It sounds almost insultingly simple: make things memorable. But I've watched smart leaders at good companies invest enormous energy into goals and values that don't actually have any effect on behavior — not because they got the strategy wrong, but because they made things too complex for it to stick.
If your goals aren't memorable, they're not useful. If you have fourteen company values, people will remember three. And they won't all remember the same three.

When people can't hold something in their head, they can't use it to make decisions. They fall back on something else — their own instincts, their manager's preferences, whatever feels urgent in the moment.
Goals are a communication tool. That's it. They exist to help people decide what to work on, prioritize their time, and know what winning looks like. If your goals can't do that, they're decorative.

At Facebook for the five years I was there, we had three top-line goals: Growth, Engagement, and Revenue. Entire organizations existed to move those numbers. But the goals themselves were simple enough that anyone in the company could tell you what they were and why they mattered.

Culture is shaped by behavior. If you choose to write your values down, they should reflect the way you already operate — and they should help people make decisions when no one senior is in the room. If an engineer is choosing between two approaches and can't point to a value that helps break the tie, the values aren't working.
